keyVerseText: In the visions of God brought he me into the land of Israel, and set me upon a very high mountain, by which was as the frame of a city on the south. by which: or, upon which
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun מִבְנֶה (mibneh) derives from the root בָּנָה (bânâh), which primarily means 'to build' or 'to construct.' This root conveys both literal and figurative senses of building, such as establishing a house or family, emphasizing the act of creating or setting up something enduring. Thus, מִבְנֶה carries the foundational idea of a constructed frame or structure, highlighting not just the physical aspect of a building but also the intentional and purposeful nature of construction inherent in the root.
usageInScripture: This word appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Ezekiel 40:2, where it is translated as 'frame' in the phrase 'by which was as the frame of a city.' The singular occurrence and its translation focus on the concept of a structural outline or framework, indicating a foundational or defining element of a city’s form. This consistency suggests that מִבְנֶה emphasizes the essential framework that supports or defines a larger whole, rather than merely any building or structure.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מִבְנֶה as a frame or structure rooted in the concept of building enriches our grasp of God's sovereign design and order in creation and redemption. The term reminds believers that God is the master builder who establishes and sustains His people and His purposes with intentionality and strength. In a Christ-centered perspective, this word points to the spiritual framework God provides for His church, built upon the firm foundation of Christ Himself. Recognizing this helps believers appreciate the stability and security found in God's constructed plan, encouraging faith in His ongoing work of building His kingdom.
keyVerseReflection: Ezekiel 40:2 describes a vision where the prophet is set upon a high mountain 'by which was as the frame of a city on the south.' The use of מִבְנֶה here conveys the idea of an essential structural outline that defines the city’s form and location. This word highlights the ordered and purposeful nature of the vision, suggesting that what Ezekiel sees is not random but divinely framed. It invites reflection on God's sovereign design and the spiritual realities underlying the physical imagery.
